title: Oncall deckhand log: TTFB arc detection and mitigation (night shift)
content:
Summary:

Night shift on 2026-03-26 (00:12–04:40 UTC) we observed repeated short-duration TTFB spikes affecting the hosted API (primarily streaming endpoints). Symptoms were a sawtooth TTFB pattern: p95 rising from baseline ~90ms to ~450–900ms for ~30–90s windows, recurring every ~4–6 minutes in affected regions. Customer-visible impact: streaming clients saw delayed first-chunk delivery and intermittent client disconnects. Total error rate did not materially increase (5xx unchanged), which made initial detection subtle.

Why this doc exists: capture the live sleuth notes from oncall, surface a correlated but non-obvious root cause (telemetry exporter backpressure -> multiplexer stall), and propose concrete runbook changes so responders can faster-triage similar future events.

Immediate detection and triage timeline (concise):
- 00:12 UTC: Pager triggered (latency alert: hosted-api/region-eu p95 TTFB > 300ms for 2m).
- 00:15 UTC: Oncall (Aisha) confirms p95 and p98 spikes on the TTFB dashboard; 5xx and request volume stable.
- 00:18 UTC: Quick check shows streaming sessions count steady but first-byte latency spiking; edge proxies (edge-proxy clusters A,B) CPU modestly elevated.
- 00:22 UTC: Deployed temporary Synthetic Flag: route 10% of traffic to fallback multiplexer cluster (mux-b) — no material change to spike frequency.
- 00:28 UTC: Correlation discovered: internal telemetry ingestion (trace-proxy) spiked in CPU + queue depth concurrently with TTFB spikes.
- 00:35 UTC: Hypothesis formed: trace-proxy exporter backpressure creating ephemeral contention inside multiplexer process due to shared event loop.
- 00:40 UTC: Mitigation 1: throttle telemetry sampling at ingress (revert live-refined sampling from 1:1 to 1:50) via rapid feature flag. TTFB spikes amplitude reduced within 90s.
- 01:05 UTC: Mitigation 2: scaled trace-proxy deployment by 2x in affected region, rolled exporter-side retry/backoff fix to reduce synchronous flushes (hotfix PR).
- 02:20 UTC: System stabilized to baseline for 24+ hours of observation in EU region.

Impact summary:
- User-facing: increased first-byte latency and occasional streaming session resets for ~20% of sessions during spike windows. No sustained 5xx wave, so downstream platform fallbacks were rarely triggered. Estimated affected requests: ~2.8% of total request volume for EU region over the 3 hour window.
- Business: No major customer escalations; a few internal alerts from volume-sensitive customers.
- Internal ops: Oncall time ~3.5 hours; engineering time for follow-ups ~10 engineer-hours across infra and telemetry teams.

Root cause (short):
- Primary cause: telemetry ingestion pipeline (trace-proxy) experienced periodic CPU/queue pressure when recent sampling configuration increased synchronous exporter flushes. The trace-proxy shares the same multiplexing runtime process or uses a tight RPC path that competes with streaming request event loop scheduling on edge/mux. The exporter backpressure induced short pauses in the multiplexer that delayed first-chunk writes (TTFB).

Contributing factors:
- Recent telemetry config change staged last week increased span sampling for debug windows (1:1) in EU while troubleshooting unrelated tracing gaps.
- Trace-proxy exporter implementation contained synchronous flush calls on sampling boundary (no async handoff), which amplified CPU spikes during bursts.
- Multiplexer and telemetry agent share CPU affinity / cgroup assignment on some instance types used in the EU rollout (not isolated).
- Existing alerting focused on 5xx and overall latency percentiles but did not have a dedicated TTFB playbook or early-warning synthetic checks for first-chunk delays.

Why this is different from a standard "server-saturated" incident:
- Resource charts (cpu/io) looked 'ok' at coarse granularity because these were short bursts; only high-resolution sampling (1s-5s) showed the contention. Some older runbooks assume sustained CPU/heap leaks — here it was a telemetry-induced microburst pattern.

Immediate remediation performed:
- Rapid rollback of sampling config (feature flag roll-back) to reduce telemetry ingress rate.
- Short-term scaling of trace-proxy replicas in EU (scale + manual pod eviction to rebalance).
- Added exporter-side backoff quick-fix (hotfix PR linked) to avoid synchronous blocking on flush.
- Increased TTFB alert sensitivity and added a transient rule that suppresses noise but surfaces repeated 2m windows.

Longer-term action items (owner, ETA, notes):
1) Remove synchronous flushes from trace exporter and add bounded async buffer (owner: Marco Nguyen, ETA: 2026-04-10). Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/telemetry/pull/412
2) Hard CPU isolation: ensure multiplexer, edge-proxy and trace-proxy processes run with distinct CPU sets on EU instance profiles (owner: Leah Kim, ETA: 2026-05-01).
3) Rollback safe sampling policy: create a canary rollout path with gradual sampling increase and auto-rollback on TTFB metric drift (owner: Observability, ETA: 2026-04-24).
4) Runbook update: add TTFB triage checklist and 1s-resolution dashboards; include common telemetry-induced hypotheses (owner: Aisha Patel, ETA: 2026-03-31).
5) Synthetic test: add first-byte synthetic probe (streaming) that measures initial-chunk latency every 30s across all regions (owner: SRE devex, ETA: 2026-04-15).
6) Postmortem review and blameless retro (owner: Diego Morales, ETA: 2026-04-05).

Runbook triage checklist (PROTOCOL) — immediate steps for oncall when TTFB spikes are detected:
1) Confirm p95/p98 TTFB on streaming route (dashboard: TTFB-streaming-region).
2) Check 1s-resolution CPU and event-loop latency for edge-proxy and multiplexer processes.
3) Query trace-proxy queue depth and exporter flush latency (query examples below).
4) Check recent telemetry sampling flags / toggles in the flags dashboard (who changed it).
5) If trace-proxy queue depth > 1000 or exporter flush > 50ms, reduce sampling (feature flag) to baseline and watch for improvement for 90–120s.
6) If suppression does not reduce spikes, scale trace-proxy (x2) and temporarily route a small percentage of traffic to fallback mux cluster.
7) Open a postmortem issue and notify observability + infra teams.

Diagnostic queries / commands (copy-able):
- High-resolution TTFB: SELECT time, p95_ttfb FROM metrics.ttfb_streaming WHERE region='eu' AND time > now()-10m GROUP BY time(1s);
- Trace-proxy queue depth: curl -s http://trace-proxy-eu:9090/metrics | grep queue_depth;
- Exporter flush latency (histogram): curl -s http://trace-proxy-eu:9090/metrics | grep exporter_flush_ms_bucket;
- Event-loop blocking: kubectl exec -c mux -it mux-pod -- /bin/tooling/eventloop-stats --window=1s

Notes from the field (oncall flavor):
- 00:26 — small victory: noticed trace-proxy logs with repeated "flushing batch n=256" spikes at same cadence as TTFB. Felt like a smoking gun once we overlayed traces.
- 00:33 — tried a quick 10% route to mux-b; no change. That helped rule out a single mux host crash and pointed back to a shared dependency (telemetry).
- 00:37 — the sampling flag owner was paged (observability engineer), helpful to quickly confirm the config change last week. That cut the candidate list dramatically.
- 00:42 — throttling sampling led to a visible reduction in exporter flushes within 30–60s and TTFB amplitude dropped. Minimal customer impact after that.
- 01:12 — trace-proxy scaling took longer than expected due to image pull throttling in EU region; file a follow-up to ensure warm pool of trace-proxy exists.

Open questions / unresolved points:
- Why did the trace-proxy exporter use synchronous flush path in production? (Design/legacy reason). Need deeper code review and backlog ticket.
- Why did the recent sampling change go to 1:1 in EU without the canary safeguards described in the product observability charter? Was human error or missing guardrails?
- Are there other shared dependencies that can create similar microburst interference patterns (e.g., metrics exporter, KMS token refresh) — catalogue and test.

Suggested runbook language to add (short):
- \"If TTFB spikes without 5xx increase, check telemetry ingestion as a candidate. Specifically: trace-proxy queue depth and exporter flush histogram. If exporter flush 95th > 30ms, immediately reduce sampling and consider scaling trace-proxy before touching mux or edge hosts.\"

Follow-ups created (links):
- JIRA SRE-2145: \"TTFB spikes caused by telemetry exporter backpressure\" (assigned Diego Morales).
- GH Telemetry PR 412: async exporter buffer (linked).
- Infra Run: create CPU affinity policy for mux/trace processes (ticket INFRA-1383).

Lessons learned (blameless):
- Telemetry pipelines are now a first-class infrastructure dependency for latency-sensitive streaming; treat them similarly to kernel-level daemons — avoid synchronous cross-cutting flushes.
- Alerting must include first-byte latency for streaming endpoints at higher resolution (1s windows) to catch microbursts.
- Operational guardrails (canary rollouts, automated safeguards) for telemetry sampling are essential to avoid human-error-induced blast radius.

Appendix: logs and snippets (sanitized)
- trace-proxy-eu logs (excerpt):
  [00:25:12] exporter: flushing batch size=256 duration_ms=74
  [00:25:18] exporter: flushing batch size=256 duration_ms=81
  [00:25:24] exporter: flushing batch size=256 duration_ms=67

- mux event-loop sample (1s window):
  00:25:13: event_loop_blocked=52ms
  00:25:18: event_loop_blocked=89ms
  00:25:24: event_loop_blocked=61ms

- quick checklist used (night):
  * Confirm metric -> check cpu/event-loop -> check trace-proxy -> reduce sampling -> scale trace-proxy -> observe 2m -> update incident ticket

Closing note:
Thanks to the observability team for rapid rollback of the sampling flag and to infra for scaling support. This incident exposed an orthogonal class of reliability failure (telemetry-induced microbursts). Documenting the troubleshooting path here so future responders can move from detection to remediation in minutes rather than hours.

Signed-off-by: Aisha Patel (oncall)
